strengths: The paper presents a coherent and well-motivated reframing of reward inference as a three-stage 'audit' (posterior recovery, uncertainty diagnostics, policy-level validation), which is a sensible and clearly articulated structure for alignment auditing.

Experiments cover multiple model scales (Pythia, SmolLM, Llama-3.2-1B) and report a broad set of metrics (pairwise accuracy, AUROC, Brier, ECE, MI, log-det covariance, downstream toxicity reduction), including error bars in the policy-level comparison.

The policy-level validation (Stage 3) is a genuine strength: demonstrating that the inferred reward can drive PPO to achieve toxicity reductions comparable to the oracle reward, and that the under-identified round-1 posterior induces reward hacking, provides a functional end-to-end check that goes beyond reward-model fit metrics.
Qualitative appendix tables (rounds 1–5) concretely illustrate the reward-hacking vs. healthy alignment contrast, making the claims tangible.
The limitations section is honest and correctly identifies the linear/frozen-feature restriction and the classifier-proxy evaluation as key constraints.
weaknesses: Limited technical novelty. The core machinery — Bayesian IRL with a Bradley–Terry likelihood, mean-field Gaussian variational inference, and sequential posterior-as-prior updates — is textbook material (Ramachandran & Amir 2007; Choi & Kim 2011), and Cai et al. (2025) already apply variational Bayesian IRL to LLM alignment. The paper's contribution is essentially a framework/aggregation of known components, and the sequential update scheme is not a methodological advance: partitioning data into K rounds and observing monotone posterior contraction largely restates the fact that more data narrows a posterior.

Circular, self-referential evaluation. The 'ground-truth' reward is a RoBERTa toxicity classifier; the expert policies are trained with that same classifier; the inferred reward is then validated against that same classifier. This demonstrates recovery of a single known, linear-like reward on a synthetic setup rather than auditing genuinely opaque objectives. Claims about auditing real LLMs for 'safety teams and regulators' are substantially stronger than the evidence.

No baseline comparisons. There is no comparison against obvious alternatives: a point-estimate (MLE) reward model, bootstrap/ensemble uncertainty baselines, Cai et al. (2025), or standard reward-model training. Without these, it is impossible to judge whether the Bayesian machinery (vs. any generic uncertainty estimate) is responsible for the diagnostics or downstream gains.

The pairwise inference task may be trivially easy: o+ and o− are generated by two different policies, so a linear head over frozen embeddings can likely separate them by style/policy artifacts rather than by recovering the toxicity objective. The paper does not rule out this confound.

The headline OOD result (r=0.989 correlation between reward variance and Mahalanobis distance) is close to tautological for a linear-Gaussian model — posterior variance grows predictably with distance from the training feature distribution — and is presented as a substantive empirical finding.

Narrow scope: a single task (detoxification) on a single dataset (RealToxicityPrompts), 20-token continuations, models up to 1B. Generalization claims to helpfulness, factuality, bias, and regulatory use are speculative.
No discussion of code/data release or hyperparameter sensitivity (α, σ0, number of rounds), which limits reproducibility of the full pipeline (PPO expert training + VI + downstream RLHF).

The claim that sequential updates 'mitigate reward hacking' may partly be an artifact of data partitioning (round 1 simply has the fewest samples); a controlled comparison (e.g., one-shot inference on the full dataset) is not clearly reported.

strengths: The paper is clearly written and well-organized, presenting a complete three-stage pipeline (posterior recovery, uncertainty diagnostics, policy-level validation) with an accessible formalization (Secs. 3-4) and reproducible algorithmic details (Algorithms 1-2).

The end-to-end experimental design is thorough for its scope: six models across a range of scales, sequential Bayesian updates with posterior contraction tracking, epistemic uncertainty probes, and an RLHF-based policy-level validation rather than stopping at reward-estimation metrics.

The finding that the under-identified round-1 posterior induces reward hacking while contracted posteriors do not is a concrete, interpretable result connecting identifiability to downstream alignment behavior, supported by qualitative tables.
The limitations section is candid about the linear reward family, frozen features, classifier-based proxy ground truth, and small/mid-scale setup.
weaknesses: Limited technical novelty: the method is a standard Bayesian IRL pipeline (isotropic Gaussian prior, Bradley-Terry likelihood, mean-field Gaussian VI, sequential posterior-as-prior updates) applied to a linear head over frozen embeddings. Each component is well-established, and sequential Bayesian updating with expected posterior contraction is textbook behavior rather than a methodological contribution.

The setup is close to trivial/circular: with prompt-matched expert vs. baseline completions from an oracle toxicity classifier, the 'reward inference' task reduces to logistic regression on feature differences between two easily separable completion pools. High pairwise accuracy and clean toxic/non-toxic separation are therefore largely guaranteed and do not evidence meaningful 'auditing.' Crucially, real auditing scenarios lack access to the ground-truth objective; here the entire validation loop is defined against a known oracle, undermining the central claim of auditing real, opaque objectives.

Missing baselines and ablations: no comparison to a simple non-Bayesian point estimate (MLE/logistic regression), ensembles, or prior Bayesian reward-modeling methods (e.g., Yang et al. 2024; Cai et al. 2025) on the same task. Without these, it is impossible to know what the Bayesian machinery adds over standard practice.

Some headline diagnostics are near-tautological: the r=0.989 correlation between reward variance and Mahalanobis distance follows almost directly from the linear-Gaussian model (variance grows quadratically with distance from the mean), and increased uncertainty on 'marked'/OOD prompts is the expected behavior of any posterior over a linear model, not evidence of a novel capability.

Narrow empirical scope: a single task (detoxification), a single reward structure (linear), a single ground-truth proxy (RoBERTa toxicity classifier), and models up to 1B parameters. The broad framing ('auditors, safety teams, and regulators', 'general blueprint for alignment auditing') is significantly overclaimed relative to this evidence, and the limitations section does not resolve this gap.

Statistical rigor is uneven: most quantitative figures (e.g., Fig. 3, sequential-round metrics in Fig. 4) lack error bars or seeds; only Fig. 5 reports mean ± std over 5 runs. Qualitative analysis rests on just two prompts ([2] and [5]) across all appendix tables, raising cherry-picking concerns.

The core empirical takeaway (more data yields a better reward model, which in turn reduces reward hacking in PPO) is unsurprising, and the paper does not isolate which element of the framework—Bayesian posterior, sequential rounds, or simply more preference pairs—drives the improvement.

Positioning vs. closest work (Cai et al. 2025, variational Bayesian IRL for LLM alignment) is thin: the claimed distinction ('broader auditing framework') is primarily a framing change rather than a demonstrated technical or empirical advantage.

strengths: The reframing of reward inference from one-shot estimation to a multi-stage 'auditing process' (posterior recovery → uncertainty diagnostics → policy-level validation) is well-motivated and clearly articulated, addressing the genuine and important problem of non-identifiability in IRL for LLMs.

The evaluation covers all three claimed stages: calibration/reward-separation analysis, sequential posterior contraction with epistemic uncertainty tracking, and downstream RLHF validation, which is more complete than many IRL-for-LLM papers that stop at inference.

Experiments span multiple model scales (Pythia, SmolLM, Llama-3.2-1B), providing a scaling analysis of identifiability, and qualitative appendix tables convincingly illustrate the round-1 reward-hacking failure mode versus later-round coherent outputs.

The observation that under-identified (round-1) posteriors induce reward hacking during PPO while contracted posteriors avoid it is an interesting and practically relevant finding connecting identifiability to downstream alignment safety.
The framework, algorithms, and hyperparameters are described in enough detail (Algorithms 1-2, implementation details) to be broadly reproducible.
weaknesses: Limited technical novelty: the core machinery is a standard mean-field variational Bradley-Terry reward model with sequential Bayesian updates (posterior-as-prior), which is textbook Bayesian modeling. Closely related Bayesian reward/IRL work for LLMs already exists (Yang et al. 2024; Cai et al. 2025; Melo et al. 2024), and the delta over these is primarily framing plus a trivially expected result—posterior contraction with more data—rather than a new method.

Circular evaluation setup undermines the central 'auditing' claim: the expert policy πE is trained by the authors using a known reward R* (a toxicity classifier), and the audit then 'recovers' that same reward. This is a self-referential recovery task on a proxy reward, not an audit of an actual opaque production LLM's objectives; the strong claims about auditors, safety teams, and regulators are therefore much broader than the evidence.

The inferred reward is effectively a linear toxicity classifier over frozen mean-pooled embeddings trained on expert-vs-baseline pairs; the paper does not include the natural baseline of a plain (non-Bayesian) Bradley-Terry MLE reward model, ensembles, or bootstrap uncertainty, so it is unclear what the Bayesian machinery adds over simpler alternatives.

The headline OOD diagnostic (r=0.989 correlation between reward variance and Mahalanobis distance) is largely an artifact: for a Gaussian posterior over linear rewards, Var[R(o)] = φ(o)ᵀΣφ(o) grows with feature norm/distance essentially by construction, so this does not demonstrate genuine 'self-aware' uncertainty; the shortcut-detection probe is also a single, simple keyword-injection test.

Narrow empirical scope: one task (detoxification), one dataset (RealToxicityPrompts), one reward family (linear), and models at most 1B parameters. The generalization claims ('blueprint for alignment auditing', applicability to helpfulness/factuality/bias) are unsupported.

Several methodological details are missing or unclear (feature dimensionality, sensitivity to α, temperature of RLHF expert training, number of paired demonstrations, how the 5 data rounds are split), and there are no ablations on K, prior variance σ0, or the choice of encoder—key knobs for identifiability claims.

Presentation issues: numerous typos and inconsistencies (e.g., '3 PRELIMINARIES.', duplicated sentence fragments in Implementation Details, text referencing Figure 5 for results shown in Figure 4), which suggest the manuscript was not carefully polished.

strengths: The paper is clearly written and well-motivated: recasting reward inference as a three-stage auditing process (posterior recovery, uncertainty diagnostics, policy-level validation) is a coherent and sensible framing for alignment auditing.

The evaluation pipeline is unusually complete for this area: preference fidelity, calibration (Brier/ECE), epistemic/aleatoric decomposition, posterior contraction tracking, OOD/shortcut probes, RLHF training dynamics, and qualitative outputs across multiple model scales (Pythia, SmolLM, Llama-1B/8B) and two tasks.

The policy-level validation is a genuinely useful contribution: showing that a round-1 (under-identified) posterior induces reward hacking during PPO while contracted posteriors (rounds 2-5) track oracle training dynamics is a concrete, interpretable demonstration that identifiability matters for downstream alignment.

The comparison in Appendix E.4 (posterior variance vs. posterior-mean reward vs. output-only toxicity signals for detecting spurious markers, AUC ~0.86-0.88 vs ~0.56) cleanly isolates the value of auditing latent reward uncertainty over output-level auditing.

Honest limitations section (linear head, frozen features, classifier-based proxy ground truth, small/mid-scale models) and a useful qualitative appendix showing degenerate vs. fluent completions per round.
weaknesses: Limited technical novelty: the core method combines standard components — Bayesian IRL with a Bradley-Terry likelihood, mean-field Gaussian VI with reparameterization, and posterior-as-prior sequential updates on a partitioned dataset. Sequential Bayesian updating is textbook; 'demonstrating posterior contraction' with more data is an expected outcome, not a discovery. The claimed advance over Cai et al. (2025) and Yang et al. (2024) is mostly framing (auditing vs. estimation), supported only by a qualitative positioning table (Appendix F), not by empirical head-to-head comparisons.

No quantitative baselines in the experiments. There is no comparison against MCMC, ensembles, MAP estimation, or Cai et al.'s variational BIRL on the same data; Table 4 is a feature checklist. The single-round vs. sequential ablation shows accuracy is essentially unchanged (0.7597 vs 0.7524 pairwise), and the log-det gap (-196 vs -897) is hard to interpret without normalizing for the accumulated prior information, weakening the claim that sequential updates are the key driver.

The 'ground-truth' audit target is itself a proxy (a RoBERTa toxicity classifier), and the reward is fit on the LLM's own mean-pooled embeddings with a linear head — so the framework recovers a linear readout of a classifier, which is a comparatively easy identification problem. Evidence that the framework audits genuinely opaque objectives (e.g., RLHF-trained models with non-linear, multi-objective rewards) is absent, yet the abstract claims a toolkit for regulators to 'verify what LLMs are truly trying to achieve.'

The context is heavily simplified: one-step contextual bandit with ~20-token completions, paired demonstrations from an expert policy the authors themselves train. This is far from auditing a third-party deployed LLM, where obtaining matched expert/baseline pairs over the same prompts — the core data requirement — may be infeasible. Practical applicability of the audit protocol in a real auditing setting is not demonstrated.

Generality claims are only weakly supported: on the helpfulness task, gains are marginal (pairwise accuracy 0.725 -> 0.729, AUROC flat at 0.70), ECE worsens with scale, and — importantly — Stage 3 (policy-level validation), the paper's strongest evidence, is not run on helpfulness. The framework is effectively validated end-to-end on one task only.

Reproducibility gaps: the 'Code available at:' field on page 1 is empty; key hyperparameters (number of rounds, dataset sizes per round, PPO details, temperature α) are only partially specified, and no significance tests or confidence intervals accompany most reported metrics despite small differences being interpreted as trends.

Some results are under-explained or potentially problematic: pairwise Brier slightly worsens with scale (0.0528 -> 0.0560, Table 2) while the text claims calibration improves; the Pythia-70M expert 'over-shifted' (very high KL) and is retained as an expert despite acknowledged training instability; the r=0.989 uncertainty-distance correlation is largely driven by the constructed marked/clean split rather than a natural OOD distribution.

strengths: The three-stage framing of reward inference as an 'audit process' (posterior recovery, uncertainty diagnostics, policy-level validation) is well-motivated and clearly presented, and the paper is generally well-organized and readable.

The policy-level validation (Stage 3) is a genuinely good idea: showing that the inferred reward can drive RLHF and replicate oracle training dynamics, and demonstrating that an under-identified round-1 posterior induces reward hacking while contracted posteriors do not, is a meaningful empirical observation.

Reasonably broad experimental coverage: multiple model families/scales (Pythia, SmolLM, Llama-1B/8B), a second task (HH-RLHF helpfulness), ablations (single-round vs. sequential), calibration metrics, and qualitative tables of completions.

Appendix E.4 provides a useful comparison against output-only auditors, showing posterior variance outperforms both output toxicity probability and posterior-mean reward at detecting spurious markers.
weaknesses: Limited technical novelty. The core method is a Bayesian logistic reward model over frozen linear features fitted by mean-field VI with a Bradley–Terry likelihood — essentially standard preference/reward learning. Sequential 'posterior-as-prior' updates over disjoint data chunks are just ordinary online Bayesian updating; observing monotonic posterior contraction as more data arrives is the expected behaviour of any Bayesian posterior, not a discovered phenomenon. The paper presents this as 'systematically reducing non-identifiability', which overclaims.

Evaluation circularity undermines the central claim of 'auditing what an LLM is truly optimizing'. The ground-truth reward is a RoBERTa toxicity classifier, expert completions are generated against that same classifier, and inferred reward quality is scored against it. Recovering a signal that separates toxic from non-toxic text in a linear head over the LLM's own embeddings is close to a supervised classification exercise, not evidence of recovering a latent training objective.

Missing empirical baselines. There is no comparison against a standard reward model (e.g., an MLP over the same features), standard preference learning, DPO-based inference, or the closest prior work (Cai et al., 2025; Yang et al., 2024) on the same data. Table 4 is a qualitative positioning table, not an empirical comparison, so the claimed advantage over prior Bayesian IRL/LLM methods is unsupported.

The 'actionable diagnostics' results are close to tautological: a linear Gaussian posterior's predictive variance grows with feature norms, which correlate with Mahalanobis distance from the training pool, so the r=0.989 correlation is largely a mathematical property of the model rather than evidence of 'self-aware' uncertainty. Likewise, the spurious-keyword probes validate behaviour the authors explicitly injected.

The sequential rounds are a passive, arbitrary partition of a static dataset, not the 'active auditing' implied in the positioning (Appendix F). No uncertainty-guided data collection is performed, so the 'sequential active auditing' novelty claim is overstated.

Results on the generalization task are weak: pairwise accuracy improves only from 0.725 to 0.729 and single-text AUROC is unchanged at 0.70 across scales, with worse ECE at 8B. This provides thin support for the 'general blueprint' framing.

Overclaiming throughout: phrases like 'verify what LLMs are truly trying to achieve' and 'the first framework to...' are not supported by a linear reward head over frozen features at ≤8B scale with a single-task oracle, as the authors themselves concede in the limitations (classifier proxy, small scale, restrictive model class).

Statistical rigor is thin for the headline Stage-3 claims: reward hacking of the round-1 posterior vs. success of rounds 2–5 is shown over 5 runs with mean±std, but no significance testing; the distinction could be sensitive to PPO variance.

Reproducibility is incomplete: the 'Code available at:' statement on page 1 is empty, and many experimental details (dataset sizes used, α, σ0, round construction, number of pairs) are underspecified.

Several presentation issues: reward scores on implausible scales (hundreds), inconsistent metric reporting between figures and appendix tables (e.g., Pairwise ECE 0.0425 vs 0.0448 in ablation text vs. Table 3), and a threshold-based single-text metric whose validation selection procedure is only sketched.

strengths: The three-stage audit framing (posterior recovery → uncertainty diagnostics → policy-level validation) is a clear and well-motivated conceptual reframing of reward inference as verification rather than one-shot estimation.

The empirical pipeline is unusually comprehensive for this area: multiple model scales (Pythia, SmolLM, Llama-1B/8B), calibration metrics (Brier, ECE, reliability curves), an ablation of single-round vs. sequential inference (Table 3), OOD/spurious-feature probes (Figures 7, 14), and qualitative reward-hacking examples across rounds (Appendix G).

The Stage 2 diagnostics are given quantitative support beyond anecdotes: the correlation between reward variance and Mahalanobis distance (r=0.989) and the comparison against an output-only auditor (Figure 14, AUC ≈ 0.86–0.88 vs ≈ 0.56) are convincing within their setting.

The observation that the round-1 (under-identified) posterior induces reward hacking while contracted posteriors do not is a genuinely interesting result linking non-identifiability to downstream safety failures.
Writing and figure presentation are generally clear, and limitations (linear head, frozen features, classifier-based ground truth) are acknowledged honestly in Appendix A.
weaknesses: Fundamental circularity in the evaluation: the 'ground truth' reward is a RoBERTa toxicity classifier, the expert policy πE is trained with that same classifier, and the recovered reward is a linear head over the same LLM's frozen features evaluated on the same dataset. The audit is thus largely a reconstruction of a reward signal the authors themselves injected into the pipeline, rather than an audit of an unknown, opaque objective. The central claim — auditing 'what LLMs truly optimize' — is only demonstrated in this synthetic, self-constructed loop, which severely limits external validity for real RLHF-aligned models.

Posterior contraction across sequential rounds is largely a mathematical inevitability: feeding i.i.d. data in rounds with posterior-as-prior updates must shrink the posterior (log det decrease) under a correctly specified model. The paper treats monotonic contraction as evidence of 'systematic non-identifiability reduction,' but no experiment tests the more meaningful case (e.g., conflicting evidence rounds, misspecification) where the framework's diagnostic claims would be falsifiable.

Missing baselines: no comparison against alternative UQ methods for the reward (deep ensembles, MC dropout, Laplace approximation on the linear head), nor against a standard non-Bayesian reward model of the same capacity. The only baseline in E.4 is an output-only toxicity probability, which is a weak strawman. Table 4 is a qualitative positioning table, not an empirical comparison.

The second task (helpfulness) is under-validated: gains are marginal (0.725→0.729 pairwise accuracy), ECE does not improve, and crucially Stage 3 (policy-level RLHF validation) is not run on helpfulness, so the strongest claim of the framework is only established on the single, synthetic toxicity setting.

Novelty is modest at the technical level: Bayesian IRL with Bradley–Terry likelihood and mean-field VI is standard, and sequential Bayesian updating is textbook; the contribution is primarily packaging/framing. Cai et al. (2025) already do variational BIRL for LLM alignment; the delta (sequential rounds + diagnostics) is incremental.

The linear reward over frozen mean-pooled embeddings is restrictive and the diagnostics may largely reflect geometry of the embedding space rather than reward ambiguity (e.g., the strong variance–Mahalanobis correlation may be an artifact of the linear-Gaussian setup, Var[R(o)] = φ(o)ᵀΣφ(o)).

Reproducibility concerns: the code link on page 1 is empty ('Code available at:'), and several experimental details are underspecified (dataset sizes per round, number of preference pairs, α value, how spurious markers are constructed, variance of Figure 7 error bars).

Some overclaiming relative to evidence: 'first framework to integrate IRL with sequential active auditing', 'verify what LLMs are truly trying to achieve', and the abstract's suggestion of regulatory usefulness — the setting is small-scale models with a proxy classifier reward, 20-token completions, and no human evaluation.
